02Android platform — concept

Analogy: Android is the building; apps are the shops inside.

02Platform picture

The picture is a stack: apps on top, framework in the middle, Linux kernel underneath — matching the notes’ “unified platform” story.

  • Mobile OS by Google, based on the Linux kernel
  • Built mainly for touchscreen phones & tablets
  • Unified APIs → one development approach across devices
  • Your code talks to the application framework (not the kernel directly)
  • Beginner pitfall: thinking Android is “just an app store” — it is a full OS
Classroom hook Same APIs on a budget phone or a flagship — that is the unified pitch from Unit-2.

03AOSP — concept

When people say “Android is open,” they mean AOSP.

Kernel
Linux underneath
Middleware
Powers the device
Framework
3rd-party apps live here

03AOSP — open layers

What did Google give away for free? Click
Code for low-level “stuff”, middleware to power a device, and a full application framework so third-party apps can be built, installed, and run.
What does “Android is open” mean? Click
The Android Open Source Project (AOSP) — free to use: write code, build the OS, ship devices, make apps.
Exam phrase: Android is open-source via AOSP — not “because phones are cheap.”

06Android Studio — concept

Official IDE — one download to start building.

06Studio includes SDK + emulators

🧰

SDK

Software Development Kit with the Android libraries you need — bundled so you are not hunting packages by hand.

📲

Emulators

Infrastructure to download emulator (AVD) instances — run apps without a real device on day one.

⚡

Official IDE

Google’s recommended tool — write XML/Java, preview layouts, build, and debug in one place.

Do I need a physical phone on day 1? Click
No. Emulators (AVDs) let you run apps virtually. Real devices are great later for sensors and performance.

07JDK & environment — concept

07Setup stepper — JDK → JAVA_HOME → Studio

Tap each step. Follow along on your laptop.

1 Install JDK (Oracle)
Download the latest Java Development Kit from oracle.com and install it. Android tools need a JDK to compile Java projects.
2 Set JAVA_HOME / environment variables
This PC → Properties → Advanced System Settings → Environment Variables → New. Variable value = path where the JDK is installed. Click OK.
3 Download & install Android Studio
Install latest Android Studio. When the welcome window appears — congratulations! Studio (with SDK + emulator support) is ready.
Congrats moment = welcome screen. If you see it, setup worked. 🎉
Class-safe meme break

Gradle sync vs Hello World

Expectation
🚀 Code for 2 minutes → Hello World on screen
Reality
☕ Gradle downloads the internet… then Hello World
Pro tip First sync is slow. Don’t panic. Second sync is friendlier.

08Android project — concept

08Create project — wizard steps

File → New → New Project opens the wizard.

1 File → New → New Project
Opens the new application wizard. An Android project contains the files that make up an application.
2 Name + package (reverse DNS)
Enter app name and package. Package uses reverse DNS — domain reversed + identifiers.
3 Device + min SDK
Select devices and minimum SDK. Defaults are fine for our first project.
4 Activity template → Finish
Notes start with no activity, then add later. Click Finish — project created!

09Package name — reverse DNS concept

From the notes Package like com.example.raazu.myapplication — organization domain flipped, then app identifiers.

10Device, SDK & templates

Device + min SDK

Pick phone/tablet plus minimum SDK. Defaults are OK for learning. Wizard may look slightly different after Studio updates.

Activity templates

Empty Activity, Basic, etc. Notes: for the first app we add no activity, then create layout + class ourselves.

Why start with “no activity”? Click
So you manually wire XML layout + Activity class + Manifest — the exam cares that you understand the links.

11Project anatomy — picture

  • res/ — layouts, values, images, audio…
  • res/layout/ — XML UI pages
  • res/values/ — strings, colors, styles
  • java/… — Activity classes
  • AndroidManifest.xml — declares components
All resource file names under res/ must be lowercase.

12Layout — concept (6Q)

Analogy: layout = room plan for one screen.

12What is a layout? — picture

The picture shows a screen “blueprint”: containers and children, not Java logic. Notes: design UI with XML; keep files in res/layout/ (Figures 2-6 / 2-7).

  • XML file under res/layout/ (create Resource type layout)
  • Describes widgets + nesting + attributes (Linear, Relative, Constraint…)
  • Not the Java logic — just the design of one page
  • Example: first.xml = vertical LinearLayout + Hello World TextView
  • Names must be lowercase — uppercase resource names fail the build
  • Mistake: editing the phone UI by hand — change the XML (or preview), then Run
TextView
Button A
Button B

13Widgets — concept

Analogy: widgets = Lego bricks.

13Widgets labeled — picture

Definition (exam-ready) Widgets are the building blocks you use to compose a user interface. A widget can show text or graphics, interact with the user, or arrange other widgets. Buttons, text inputs, and check boxes are all widgets (notes).
  • Picture ≈ notes Figure 2-8 — widgets as seen on screen
  • first.xml: LinearLayout + TextView · second.xml: adds Buttons
  • Mistake: calling only Button a “widget” — TextView and layouts count too

14Label / TextView — concept

In notes, “label” means TextView.

14TextView picture

Notes call this a Label; in XML it is a TextView. The picture highlights the attributes used in first.xml’s Hello World.

  • android:text — what to show (“Hello World!” or later @string/…)
  • textSize / textStyle — look (notes: 20sp, bold)
  • gravity — align text inside the view (center)
  • layout_marginTop — space from above (50dp in the sample)
  • Width/height: often match_parent × wrap_content for a title line
  • Mistake: forgetting layout_width/layout_height — almost every widget needs them
Hello World’s star widget is a single centered TextView inside a vertical LinearLayout.

15Create a layout file — steps

1 Create res/layout
Resources for UI live in res/. Add subfolder layout (resource type: layout).
2 New layout file: first.xml
Lowercase name. Choose LinearLayout. Click OK.
3 Add TextView “Hello World!”
Two widgets: root LinearLayout + child TextView.
Note: names of all files under the resource folder must be lowercase.

16Hello World — picture first

See it before you read XML: LinearLayout (column) + TextView.

Hello World!
Root = vertical LinearLayout · Child = TextView
  • Orientation: vertical
  • Root size: match_parent × match_parent
  • TextView height: wrap_content
  • Gravity center + bold 20sp + marginTop 50dp
Remember Our activity layout defines two widgets: a LinearLayout and a TextView.

16first.xml — explained

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<LinearLayout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    android:orientation="vertical" android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent">

     <TextView
         android:layout_width="match_parent"
         android:layout_height="wrap_content"
         android:text="Hello World!"
         android:gravity="center"
         android:textSize="20sp"
         android:textStyle="bold"
         android:layout_marginTop="50dp" />

</LinearLayout>
Root must declare the Android XML namespace. Child TextView sits inside the LinearLayout.

17Hierarchy complete picture

Completed tree for second.xml (notes Figures 2-9 & 2-10). Parent/child language: the root has two children; the inner LinearLayout has two Button children.

  • Vertical LinearLayout (root ViewGroup)
  • TextView (question) — often @string/text_question
  • Horizontal LinearLayout (child group)
  • Two Buttons (True / False) as grandchildren of the root
  • Phone mock on the right ≈ layout preview (Figure 2-11)
  • Mistake: forgetting namespace on the root — XML fails to resolve android: attributes
Root LinearLayout must declare the Android XML namespace http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android.

18second.xml — line-by-line nesting

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<LinearLayout xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent"
    android:gravity="center"
    android:orientation="vertical">
    <TextView
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="@string/text_question"
        android:textStyle="bold"
        android:textSize="20sp"/>
    <LinearLayout
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:orientation="horizontal">
        <Button android:layout_width="wrap_content"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content"
            android:text="@string/text_true"/>
        <Button android:layout_width="wrap_content"
            android:layout_height="wrap_content"
            android:text="@string/text_false"/>
    </LinearLayout>
</LinearLayout>
Nesting read Root vertical → TextView + horizontal LinearLayout → two Buttons as grandchildren.

19ViewGroup — concept

LinearLayout inherits from ViewGroup.

19ViewGroup types — tap

LinearLayout Tap
Single column or row. Use android:orientation vertical/horizontal.
FrameLayout Tap
Stack children — often one visible “frame” of content.
TableLayout Tap
Arrange widgets in rows/columns like a table.
RelativeLayout Tap
Position children relative to parent or siblings.
Parent / child Root LinearLayout has two children: TextView + horizontal LinearLayout. That child layout has two Button children.

20Attributes — concept

20match_parent vs wrap_content — animate

layout_width / layout_height are required for almost every widget. match_parent = as big as the parent; wrap_content = as big as contents need. Old docs may say fill_parent (same as match_parent). Watch the animation, then check your XML.

match_parent — as big as parent (old name: fill_parent)
width = match_parent
wrap_content — hug the text/content
Hello
orientation Tap
On LinearLayout: vertical or horizontal.
android:text Tap
Prefer @string/… references — not hard-coded literals.
Width habit
TextView often wrap_content; full-bleed rows use match_parent
Exam trap
If you write fill_parent, say it’s deprecated ≡ match_parent

21String resources — concept

21strings.xml — code

res/values/strings.xml — reference with @string/name

<resources>
    <string name="app_name">My Application</string>
    <string name="text_question">Android Studio is better than
Eclipse</string>
    <string name="text_true">True</string>
    <string name="text_false">False</string>
</resources>
Why not hardcode android:text="True"? Click
Placing strings in a separate file is better for translation, reuse, and maintenance. Reference them as @string/text_true.

Logic block

Activity, inflate,
Manifest & AVD

XML is the face. Activity is the brain. Manifest is the guest list. AVD is the fake phone.

23Activity — concept

23Activity = layout + class

Notes (Creating a New Class): a visible page needs both a layout resource and a class that extends Activity. Picture/chain below is the mental model for second.xml ↔ Second.java.

Layout (XML)

Design the page: widgets, hierarchy, attributes. Lives in res/layout/. Example: second.xml with question + True/False.

Class (Java)

Extends Activity. In onCreate you link the layout and later add events. Notes use Java (Second.java).

second.xml ← setContentView → Second.java
  • Mistake: creating only XML — nothing launches until an Activity calls setContentView
  • Mistake: forgetting to declare the Activity in AndroidManifest.xml
One-liner for exams Click
For creating pages we need a class file that extends Activity — in that class we link the layout and add functionality to widgets.

24setContentView / inflate — concept

24Second.java — code

1 Extend Activity
public class Second extends Activity — your screen is an Activity subclass.
2 Override onCreate
Called when an instance is created. Always call super.onCreate(b) first.
3 setContentView(R.layout.second)
Inflates the layout: each widget is instantiated from XML attributes, then put on screen.
package com.example.raazu.myapplication;

import android.app.Activity;
import android.os.Bundle;

public class Second extends Activity{
    @Override
    public void onCreate(Bundle b){
        super.onCreate(b);
        setContentView(R.layout.second);
    }
}

25Resources & R — concept

25R.java IDs — tap

R.layout.second Tap
ID for res/layout/second.xml — passed to setContentView.
R.string.app_name Tap
Example in code: setTitle(R.string.app_name);
Where do IDs live? Tap
Generated in R.java — don’t hand-edit; rebuild regenerates it.
res/ folders Tap
Layouts → res/layout · Strings → res/values · Images → res/drawable (etc.)

26Manifest — concept

Analogy: Manifest = guest list for the OS.

26AndroidManifest.xml — code

The Manifest is the app’s ID card for the OS and Play. Notes require declaring package, components (here .Second), and the launcher intent-filter. Mistake: perfect Activity class that never appears in this file — it will not launch.

1 Declare activity .Second
Add <activity android:name=".Second"> inside <application>.
2 Attach MAIN + LAUNCHER filter
Makes this the first/launcher activity when the app icon is tapped.
<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    package="com.example.raazu.myapplication">
  <application … >
    <activity android:name=".Second">
      <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" />
      </intent-filter>
    </activity>
  </application>
</manifest>

27Intent-filter — concept

Analogy: intent-filter = doorbell label.

27MAIN + LAUNCHER

  • Intents activate activities, services, broadcast receivers
  • System matches an intent via intent-filter declarations
  • If multiple apps can handle it → user picks
  • Activity with MAIN + LAUNCHER → first/launcher activity
Exam line If an activity is defined with an <intent-filter> for MAIN/LAUNCHER, that activity launches as the first activity of the application.
Quick check · Exercise Q9 vibes
What does MAIN + LAUNCHER in an intent-filter do?
Correct: MAIN action + LAUNCHER category tell Android this activity should appear as the launchable entry.

28AVD — concept

Analogy: AVD = fake phone on your laptop.

28Create an AVD — picture + stepper

1 Open AVD Manager
Tools → Android → AVD Manager or toolbar AVD Manager icon.
2 Create Virtual Device
Pick a hardware profile → Next.
3 System image
Pick API level. x86 images run fastest. Click Download if needed.
4 Verify → Finish
Adjust AVD properties if needed, then Finish.

29Run on the emulator

1 Click Run App
Use the toolbar Run action to start deployment.
2 Pick your virtual device
Choose the AVD from the list → press OK.
3 Watch the emulator
App builds, installs, launches — your layout appears on the virtual device.
First boot of an AVD can be slow. Second launch is usually much faster.

30Debugging mindset — discuss

Build fails? Tap
Check lowercase resource names, XML typos, missing closing tags, wrong package.
Blank screen? Tap
Did you call setContentView? Right layout ID? Activity in the Manifest?
App icon missing? Tap
MAIN + LAUNCHER intent-filter missing or on the wrong activity.
@string red? Tap
Name mismatch vs strings.xml — fix the resource name or add the string.
